figures.shows: The quantum stack as three stacked blocks with a metric box beside each: Applications (computational problems, and quantum simulation), Quantum software (digital control by gate sequences, analog control by Hamiltonian sequences), Quantum Hardware (laser controls, electronics, quantum register, detection system). The metric boxes name quality, speed or reliability against classical methods; complexity or gate count; and number of atoms, gate fidelity, quality factor and repetition rate. No numbers.
figures.confirmed_by: Applications (top block of the Quantum stack) can be divided into two groups: Quantum Simulation problems that involve the study of a quantum system, and standard computational problems.

figures.shows: Hardware components of a neutral atom quantum device: a classical computer with user interface and quantum software stack drives register actuators (cooling and trapping lasers; SLM, AOD, DDS, GPU, FPGA electronics) and processing actuators (Raman and Rydberg lasers; AOM/EOM, DDS, AWG electronics). Both act on the quantum register of atoms in tweezers, read by an EMCCD detection block that feeds back to the computer. Small photographs and a fluorescence image and a signal trace are inset. No numbers.
figures.confirmed_by: Information in the quantum register is extracted through detection of an image.

figures.shows: (a) A rendered layout of the optical set-up: trapping laser (red) reflected from an SLM, a 2D AOD for moving tweezers (purple) joined by a polarizing beam-splitter (PBS), a vacuum system with an inset of tweezer spots, a dichroic mirror sending fluorescence (green) to a camera. (b) A photograph of the vacuum-chamber assembly where the register is prepared. No numbers.
figures.confirmed_by: The trapping laser light (in red) is shaped by the spatial light modulator (SLM) to produce multiple microtraps at the focal plane of the lens (see inset).

figures.shows: Fluorescence images of tweezer arrays: twelve 2D patterns (lines, squares, rings, a cross, lattices and a heart shape; a 15 µm scale bar) and three 3D examples (a knot-like curve, a cubic lattice and a spherical shell) in boxes labeled about 103 µm by 103 µm by 99 µm. Taken from Ref [12].
figures.confirmed_by: Examples of tweezer arrays in 2D or 3D geometries, extracted from Ref [12].

figures.shows: (a) A sketch of moving one atom: a moving tweezer takes, transfers and releases an atom between two sites (time arrow). (b) The timeline of one computation cycle: register loading, then initial image, sub-register rearranging, assembled image, quantum processing (marked under 100 microseconds), final image and register readout; each image shows a grid with filled and empty sites.
figures.confirmed_by: The loading of the register being random, atoms are ﬁrst rearranged to realize a defect-free sub-register, on which the quantum processing is performed.

figures.shows: (a) A five-qubit circuit of H gates, a CNOT, controlled phase gates P(pi/2) and P(pi/4) and measurements, with an inset of laser beams addressing atoms for one gate. (b) The analog counterpart: a box labeled with the Schrodinger equation i hbar d|psi>/dt = H|psi> on all five qubits, then measurements.
figures.confirmed_by: In digital processing, a succession of gates is applied to the qubits to implement a quantum algorithm.

figures.shows: Bloch-sphere pictures. (a) For a NOT gate, a pi rotation takes |0> to |1> (top sphere) and |1> to |0> (bottom sphere). (b) For a CNOT gate, control-qubit spheres (red arrows) for |0c> and |1c>, and target-qubit spheres (blue arrows) which rotate by pi only when the control is |1c>; a red cross marks the no-rotation case. No numeric data.
figures.confirmed_by: According to the state of the control qubit (left column, in red), the target qubit (right column, in blue) is rotating by π or not

figures.shows: (a) Energy-level diagrams of the controlled-Z pulse sequence for the initial states |1c0t> and |0c1t>: pulse 1 (pi) on the control, pulse 2 (2 pi) on the target, pulse 3 (pi) on the control, with an energy shift marked on the Rydberg level. (b) A CNOT circuit built from a CZ gate with a Hadamard gate on the target before and after.
figures.confirmed_by: First a π pulse is applied on the control atom, then a 2π pulse on the target atom, and ﬁnally another π pulse on the control one.

figures.shows: Left: three 48-qubit layouts (orange nearest-neighbor 2D grid; green 2D layout with an interaction radius of 2.3 lattice units; red 3D cubic lattice with the same radius). Right: overhead (additional gates, y, 0 to about 270) against average number of 2-qubit gates per qubit (x, 1 to 4), one series per layout, four points each. Read from the plot: orange rises from about 50 at x=1 to about 262 at x=4 (about 113 at 2, about 183 at 3); green from about 14 at x=1 to about 92 at x=4 (about 38 at 2, about 67 at 3); red from about 8 at x=1 to about 41 at x=4 (about 20 at 2, about 29 at 3).
figures.confirmed_by: This is shown on the right panel, where we plot the average gate count overhead with respect to the number of two-qubit gates.

figures.shows: (a) Level diagram of a 5-pulse CCZ sequence on two controls and a target (pi, 2 pi and pi pulses, numbered 1 to 5). (b) A Toffoli (CCNOT) gate as a CCZ with a Hadamard on the target before and after. (c) The standard Toffoli decomposition into CNOTs with H, T and T-dagger gates; six CNOTs appear.
figures.confirmed_by: The Toﬀoli gate can be decomposed into a minimum of six CNOTs, with additional single qubits gates (Hadamard gates H and T (π/8) gates).

figures.shows: Three boxes under the heading Improving the capabilities of the QPUs: number of qubits (a small and a larger atom grid), computation repetition rate (a square wave of runs n, n+1, n+2) and improved processing (a laser-addressed atom plane). No numbers.
figures.confirmed_by: The three main axes of hardware developments to improve the performances of the QPUs.

figures.shows: A rendered image of a cabinet-sized instrument with a person beside it, at the top right of the page. It has no caption or label.

A two-column comparison of Analog Quantum Simulation and Digital Quantum Simulation. Resource used: Hamiltonians against Gates. Key advantages: promising hybrid quantum-classical approaches against a universal approach. Shortcomings: limited number of available configurations against requires a large number of gates. Status: quantum advantage already achieved against academic research.

A feedback loop between a quantum processor (an n-qubit register with parameterized blocks a(theta), b(theta), c(theta) and a measurement meter) and a classical optimizer (a curve of the objective <C> against theta). The measured <C> goes to the optimizer and new theta returns to the processor. No numeric data.
figures.confirmed_by: The quantum processor is used to prepare and measure a n-qubit parameterized quantum state.

figures.shows: Left: a sketch of the copper-oxide plane of a high-temperature superconductor (Cu and O atoms labeled). Right: a ribbon-model image of the hemoglobin structure. No numeric data in the images; the caption states a threshold of circuit depths of a few hundreds.
figures.confirmed_by: The left panel shows the copper-oxide plane of a high temperature superconductor [62].

figures.shows: Left: atoms as black dots with dotted disks of radius r_b around them; overlapping disks mean strong interaction. Right: the unit-disk graph with an edge between atoms closer than r_b; the red vertices form one independent set. No numbers.
figures.confirmed_by: We show on the right the corresponding graph, with the red vertices forming one independent set.

figures.shows: A layered diagram: improvements (increasing the number of atoms, the repetition rate, control over quantum information, atom-light interfacing) lead to a NISQ QPU with tailored experiments beyond classical computers, and to advanced atom-based technologies (general purpose fault-tolerant QC, quantum memories, quantum sensing, quantum repeaters). A legend lists fast classical feedback, device connectivity, atom detection, improved set of native operations and noise mitigation. No numbers.
figures.confirmed_by: Diagram showing the impact of future technological improvements on (i) the quality of our processors in the NISQ era

papers.what_it_is: A 2020 review by Pasqal and Institut d'Optique authors of neutral-atom quantum processors, covering the hardware, digital and analog operation, and the quantum simulation and NISQ computing applications, with one Cirq routing comparison.

existing.note: The text states the 5 to 10 times figure for both the 2D (green) and 3D (red) devices, and the caption gives 48 qubits and 64 random circuits per point. Reading the plot by eye (see the new from_figure assertion on Figure 8), the 2D green series is about 3 times below the orange series and the 3D red series about 6 times below it, so the 5 to 10 range matches the 3D series but the plot does not clearly show it for the 2D series. The stored value restates the paper's text correctly.
existing.certainty_reason: A result the authors (Pasqal) report about their own architecture from one simulation set.

existing.note: The paper never names HHL. It says researchers at MIT proposed, by the end of the 90s, a quantum processor for linear algebra routines (matrix inversion, eigenvalue decomposition) and cites the review [77]. The prohibitive-requirements statement is correct as stored.
existing.value: The authors state that quantum linear algebra routines for machine learning, which they attribute to researchers at MIT by the end of the 90s, need numbers of qubits and gate fidelities that are prohibitive for devices that are and will be available in the short term.
quotes: Researchers at MIT already proposed by the end of the 90s the use of a quantum processor to perform these linear algebra routines more eﬃciently
the resource requirements for their implementation in term of numbers of qubits and gate ﬁdelities is unfortunately prohibitive for devices that are and will be available in the short term.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim, with no estimate of the resources given in the paper.
existing.reader_inference: The text says MIT and cites a review; it does not say HHL by name, so the HHL link is the stored record's inference.

existing.note: Both statements are in the paper as stored. The MIS sentence cites refs [72, 74] (Pichler et al.; Serret et al.), so it is a cited prospect, not a result of this paper. Section 3.2.1 is p.21 and the MIS sentence is on p.23.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim or a claim they cite, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 8: for about 1 to about 4 average two-qubit gates per qubit, the overhead in additional gates rises from about 50 to about 262 for the nearest-neighbor two-dimensional layout, from about 14 to about 92 for the two-dimensional layout with an interaction radius, and from about 8 to about 41 for the three-dimensional cubic layout.
quotes: This is shown on the right panel, where we plot the average gate count overhead with respect to the number of two-qubit gates.
each point corresponds to an average over 64 random circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read by eye from a plot of one simulation set; a figure-only reading is never high.
assertions.reader_inference: At the plot values the nearest-neighbor series is about 3 times the green 2D series (about 50 against 14 at one gate per qubit, about 262 against 92 at four) and about 6 times the red 3D series (about 262 against 41 at four), so the text's 5 to 10 range is matched by the 3D series and not clearly by the 2D series.

assertions.value: The authors state the Figure 8 set-up: three device architectures with 48 qubits, a nearest-neighbor 2D layout, a 2D layout with an interaction (Rydberg blockade) radius of 2.3 units of lattice spacing, and a 3D cubic lattice with the same radius, compiled with Google Cirq's qubit routing compiler, each point averaged over 64 random circuits.
quotes: Implementation of random quantum circuits on three distinct device architectures with 48 qubits, illustrated on the left.
The orange layout displays nearest-neighbor connectivity in 2D, while the green layout has an interaction radius (Rydberg blockade radius) of 2.3 units of lattice spacing.
The data points were obtained using Google Cirq qubit routing compiler, and each point corresponds to an average over 64 random circuits.
The red layout corresponds to a 3D cubic lattice, with the same interaction radius.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own simulation set-up in the Figure 8 caption.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no circuit depth, gate set or error model for the random circuits, and no confidence interval for the averages.

assertions.value: The authors state that a limited connectivity forces SWAP gates, that each additional gate introduces errors along the computation, and that the relatively large connectivity of neutral atom devices allows this effect to be mitigated.
quotes: Circumventing this problem requires the introduction of SWAP gates [15], that exchange locally the quantum state between diﬀerent qubits.
This gate addition comes at a high cost, as each additional gate introduces errors along the computation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement; the quantitative support is the Figure 8 simulation only.

assertions.value: The authors report that Rabi oscillations in atomic registers have been observed with an extremely high contrast [17, 18], corresponding to single-qubit gate fidelities F higher than 99.5%.
quotes: In atomic registers they have been observed with an extremely high contrast [17, 18], corresponding to single-qubit gate ﬁdelities F higher than 99.5%.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (refs [17, 18]).

assertions.value: The authors state that the experimentally achieved two-qubit gate fidelity has been measured to be F = 94.1% [21] and will be largely improved.
quotes: The experimentally achieved ﬁdelities have been measured to be F = 94.1% [21] and will be largely improved.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (ref [21]).
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence follows the Rydberg CNOT discussion and does not say which gate or which group measured 94.1%; ref [21] is Levine et al. 2018, per the reference list.

assertions.value: The authors state that following the Box 1 protocol the gate can be performed within 1 µs, leading to a 1 MHz clock rate for the QPU.
quotes: the gate can be performed within 1 µs, leading to a 1 MHz clock rate for the QPU.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product, with no measurement shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that current imperfection levels in the experiment allow more than a hundred gates within the typical coherence time of the system.
quotes: Current imperfection levels in the experiment allow us to perform more than a hundred gates within the typical coherence time of the system.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product, with no measurement shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the current generation of devices the clock rate (1 MHz) and the acquisition rate (5 Hz) of a neutral atom QPU are relatively small in comparison to other quantum computing platforms.
quotes: the clock rate (relative to the computation, 1 MHz) and the acquisition rate (relative to the measurement, 5 Hz) in a neutral atom QPU are relatively small in comparison to other quantum computing platforms.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of their own platform in Section 2.2.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that a Toffoli gate can be achieved with a sequence of only 7 pulses (2 Hadamard gates on both sides of a 5-pulse CCZ), and that platforms without a native Toffoli gate need not less than six Controlled-NOT gates and 9 single-qubit gates.
quotes: a Toﬀoli gate can be achieved with a sequence of only 7 pulses (2 Hadamard gates on both sides of a 5-pulse CCZ
one has to combine not less than six Controlled-NOT gates and 9 single-qubit gates to achieve the same eﬀect
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product; the gate counts are stated, not measured.
assertions.reader_inference: The 7-pulse count is a pulse count, the 6 CNOT plus 9 single-qubit count is a gate count; the paper compares them through the Figure 9 caption's more than 30 laser pulses.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Toffoli decomposition into a minimum of six CNOTs with additional single-qubit gates is equivalent to a total of more than 30 laser pulses.
quotes: This last sequence if equivalent to a total of more than 30 laser pulses.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product; no derivation of the pulse count is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that neutral atom devices present the advantage of natively implementing multi-qubit gates involving more than 2 qubits [4, 5, 17, 23], which are instrumental for several quantum algorithms including Grover search.
quotes: neutral atom devices present the advantage of natively implementing multi-qubit gates involving more that 2 qubits [4, 5, 17, 23].
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product, with citations.

assertions.value: The authors state that each tweezer can host at most one atom but does so in only about 50% of the cases, so atoms are imaged and then moved with programmable moving optical tweezers, with a success rate above 99%, to build a defect-free sub-register.
quotes: Although each tweezer can host at most one atom, it happens only in about 50% of the cases, the tweezer being empty otherwise.
tweezers, with a success rate above 99%.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product, with no data shown.
assertions.reader_inference: The 99% success rate has no citation in the sentence; it is not said whether it is per move or per register.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum processing takes less than 100 µs while the overall sequence, including loading and readout, lasts approximately 200 ms.
quotes: The processing by itself is extremely rapid since it happens in less than 100 µs, while the overall sequence, including loading and readout, lasts approximately 200 ms.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product, with no data shown.
assertions.reader_inference: Processing is under 100 µs of a cycle of about 200 ms, so the quantum step is a small part of the run time.

assertions.value: The authors state in the Figure 5 caption that moving a single atom from one site to another takes less than 1 ms.
quotes: This operation takes less than 1 ms.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product, with no data shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that detection efficiencies of more than 98.6% have been reported for the fluorescence imaging method [13], a value comparable to processors based on superconducting qubits [14].
quotes: Eﬃciencies of more than 98.6% have been reported for this detection method [13], a value comparable to processors based on superconducting qubits [14].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (refs [13, 14]).

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike in solid quantum processors such as superconducting, silicon or NV qubits, the register in an atomic QPU is not permanently built but is reconstructed after each processing, so a computation cycle has three phases: register preparation, quantum processing and register readout.
quotes: Unlike in solid quantum processors, e.g., superconducting, silicon or NV qubits, the register in an atomic QPU is not permanently built but is reconstructed after each processing.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of how its device operates.

assertions.value: The authors state that the size of the quantum register is only limited by the amount of trapping laser power and by the performance of the optical system generating the optical tweezers.
quotes: the size of the quantum register is only limited by the amount of trapping laser power and by the performance of the optical system generating the optical tweezers.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that having more qubits simply relies on increasing the number of tweezers in the interference pattern of the laser and does not involve manufacturing new chips, as it does with solid-state platforms where a key challenge is the reproducibility of each single qubit over a large device.
quotes: the laser, but does not involve manufacturing new chips as it is the case with solid-state platforms where a key challenge is the reproducibility of each single qubit over a large device.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that nature provides that all the qubits are strictly identical when taken independently, as opposed to artificial atoms such as superconducting circuits or silicon spin qubits, which they call an advantage for achieving low error rates.
quotes: Nature provides that all the qubits are strictly identical when taken independently, as opposed to artiﬁcal atoms such as superconducting circuits or Silicon spin qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that the two hyperfine ground states (F = 1 and F = 2) of the rubidium atom can serve as a digital qubit because they have very long lifetimes, of the order of tens of years.
quotes: the two hyperﬁne ground states (F = 1 and F = 2) of the rubidium atom, because they have very long lifetimes (of the order of tens of years)
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that one- and two-qubit gates are all that is needed for a universal gate set, and that arbitrary single qubit rotations together with the two-qubit CNOT gate are sufficient for any quantum algorithm [15].
quotes: one- and two-qubit gates are all that is needed to constitute a universal gate set.
the ability to realize arbitrary single qubit rotations and the wellknown two-qubit CNOT gate is suﬃcient for the realization of any quantum algorithm [15].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the result and cites a textbook [15] without proving it.

assertions.value: The authors define the fidelity F of a quantum operation as a number between 0 and 1 that measures the closeness between the state actually created by the operation and the theoretically expected state, and state that F = 99.5% corresponds to a probability of 0.5% of measuring an undesired outcome after the operation.
quotes: The ﬁdelity F of a quantum operation is a number between 0 and 1 that measures the closeness between the state actually created by the operation and the theoretically expected state.
A ﬁdelity F = 99.5% corresponds to a probability of 0.5% of measuring an undesired outcome after the operation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of F, in Section 2.2.1.
assertions.reader_inference: The second sentence treats fidelity as one minus an error probability, which holds for a gate error but is not the general definition.

assertions.value: The authors define the Rydberg blockade: two Rydberg atoms a few micrometers apart experience a dipole-dipole interaction strong enough to shift the energy of the doubly excited state, preventing the excitation of two atoms at the same time, so that the excitation of a first atom to a Rydberg state conditions the excitation of a second one.
quotes: This eﬀect is called Rydberg blockade and is the basic mechanism to achieve a quantum logic: the excitation of a ﬁrst atom to a Rydberg state conditions the excitation of a second one.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's definition of the term it uses throughout, in Section 2.2.1.

assertions.value: The authors show by a case analysis of the four input states that a sequence of a π pulse on the control, a 2π pulse on the target and a π pulse on the control realizes, within a global pi phase, the controlled-Z gate, and that CNOT follows by adding Hadamard gates on the target before and after.
quotes: This pulse sequence realizes, within a global π phase, the controlled-Z (CZ) gate
The CZ gate can then be used to generate the CNOT gate by including Hadamard gates on the target atom before and after the operation
First a π pulse is applied on the control atom, then a 2π pulse on the target atom, and ﬁnally another π pulse on the control one.
assertions.certainty_reason: A pulse-sequence argument without a stated theorem and with no error terms; the paper cites [19, 17] for the scheme.

assertions.value: The authors state that transient non-zero population of Rydberg states may lead to errors in the gate process, and that imperfections can be compensated by optimal control, which shapes the optical pulses in time and requires arbitrary waveform generators able to sample the pulses at the 100 ns timescale.
quotes: Transient non-zero population of Rydberg states may lead to errors in the process.
Practically it requires extremely fast arbitrary waveform generators that are able to sample the pulses at the 100 ns timescale.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement with no data in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the most studied analog Hamiltonian is the Ising model, obtained when the lower spin state is one of the ground states and the upper a Rydberg state, in which the coupling between two spins is of van der Waals type and depends on the inverse of the distance between them to the power of 6.
quotes: The most studied one is the Ising model, which is obtained when the |↓ state is one of the ground states and the |↑ a Rydberg state
The coupling between two spins i and j is of van der Waals type and depends on the inverse of the distance between them rij to the power of 6
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the analog Hamiltonian it implements (Eq. 1); the equation itself is not quoted because its text layer is garbled.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Ising Hamiltonian can be implemented in 1D, 2D or 3D arrays containing few hundreds of atoms, far beyond the computational capabilities of classical computers, and that it can cast computationally difficult optimization problems.
quotes: In neutral atom devices, it can be implemented in 1D, 2D or 3D arrays containing few hundreds of atoms, far beyond the computational capabilities of classical computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that two Rydberg atoms interact by the electric dipole-dipole interaction whose Hamiltonian is proportional to 1/R3 (the inverse cube of the distance R), and that the flip-flop exchange mechanism exhibits a 1/R3 scaling law and is called dipolar interaction.
quotes: whose Hamiltonian Vdd is proportional to 1/R3, with R the distance between the two atoms [30].
This exchange mechanism, also known as "ﬂip-ﬂop", exhibits a 1/R3 scaling law and is
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's definition of dipolar interaction in Box 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that, at second order of perturbation theory, the pair state of two atoms in the same S state experiences a van der Waals energy shift proportional to the inverse sixth power of the distance, with a prefactor C6(n) that increases dramatically with the principal quantum number n [32].
quotes: where C6(n) is a prefactor that increases dramatically with n, the principal quantum number [32].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's definition of the van der Waals shift in Box 2, with a citation [32].
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the exponent flat as R6; the value states it in words.

assertions.value: The authors state that the XY Hamiltonian emerges when the two spin states are dipole-coupled Rydberg states such as nS and nP, that the effective field terms are then induced by a microwave field, and that the exchange interaction scales as the inverse of the distance to the power of 3.
quotes: It naturally emerges when the spin states |↓ and |↑ are two Rydberg states that are dipole-coupled, such as |nS and |nP [33, 34].
The dipolar interaction that leads to the third term scales as the inverse to the distance rij to the power of 3 (see Box 2).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the analog XY Hamiltonian it implements (Eq. 2).

assertions.value: The authors state that Rydberg atoms in optical arrays offer a quality factor Q of about ten squared (printed as Q ∼ 102 in the text layer), the ratio of coherent evolution rate over decoherence rate, because Rydberg interaction energies, typically in the tens of MHz range, are at least two orders of magnitude larger than the energy scales associated to decoherence.
quotes: they oﬀer a very favorable quality factor Q ∼ 102, given by the ratio of coherent evolution rate over the decoherence rate.
Rydberg interaction energies are typically on the tens of MHz range, at least two orders of magnitude larger than the energy scales associated to decoherence.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product, with no measurement shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that new laser systems with much higher optical power and an improved imaging system would allow the register to scale up to a few thousands of qubits, at which point the lifetime of the atoms in the sub-register, set by the residual pressure in the vacuum chamber, becomes a limitation that motivates compact cryogenic QPUs.
quotes: this would allow to scale the size of the register up to a few thousands of qubits.
Because the latter is set by the residual pressure in the vacuum chamber, it motivates another major future development: the design of QPUs in compact cryogenic environments.
assertions.certainty_reason: A prospect the authors state without data.

assertions.value: The authors state that, with high-flux atomic sources and faster assembly and imaging, the overall repetition rate is expected to improve by an order of magnitude, which would help procedures that need a very large number of repetitions, such as variational algorithms.
quotes: Overall, the repetition rate is expected to improve by an order of magnitude.
the overall increase of the repetition rate will facilitate the implementation of procedures that require a very large number of repetitions, such as variational algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: A prospect the authors state without data.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper puts the current acquisition rate at 5 Hz (Section 2.2.1), so one order of magnitude would be about 50 Hz; the paper does not say this.

assertions.value: The authors state that a quantum advantage has already been reached in the study of quantum magnetism [27, 47], and the comparison table in the same section lists the status of analog quantum simulation as quantum advantage already achieved and of digital quantum simulation as academic research.
quotes: In this regard, a quantum advantage has already been reached in the study of quantum magnetism [27, 47].
Quantum advantage already achieved
Academic research
assertions.certainty_reason: A claim the paper attributes to other work (refs [27, 47]).
assertions.reader_inference: Ref [27] is the 51-atom Harvard experiment and [47] is cited as an Ising mapping paper (the same reference as [28]); the paper does not define quantum advantage here.

assertions.value: The authors state that analog quantum simulation is not fully general but has relatively low requirements in terms of control and operation count, making it the most competitive approach to date, and that the range of applications of this approach remains limited.
quotes: This analog setting is not fully general, but corresponds to relatively low requirements in terms of control and operation count, making it the most competitive approach to date.
the range of applications of this approach remains limited.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of analog simulation in Section 3.1.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is believed that the only target Hamiltonians that can be efficiently simulated by the hybrid approach are those that share the same symmetries as the resource Hamiltonians implementable in the quantum register [52], so some models are intrinsically hard to simulate with neutral atom devices.
quotes: it is believed that the only target Hamiltonians that can be eﬃciently simulated are the ones which share the same symmetries as the resource Hamiltonians that can be implemented in the quantum register [52].
Some models are then intrinsically hard to simulate with neutral atom devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: A belief the paper attributes to other work (ref [52]).

assertions.value: The authors state that digital quantum simulation with quantum circuits made of gates is known to be universal, in the sense that any physical model of interest can be studied, and the comparison table in the same section lists its shortcoming as requiring a large number of gates.
quotes: This ﬁnal approach, called Digital Quantum Simulation, is known to be universal, in the sense that any physical model of interest can be studied.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (ref [53]).

assertions.value: The authors state that the variational nature of hybrid quantum-classical procedures renders these algorithms relatively resilient to errors [54], making them prime candidates for an implementation on NISQ devices, and that the sole use of the quantum processor is to prepare a parameterized quantum state whose measured objective estimate feeds a classical optimizer.
quotes: Importantly, the variational nature of the procedure renders these algorithms relatively resilient to errors [54], making them prime candidates for an implementation on NISQ devices.
the sole use of the quantum processor is to prepare a given quantum state, parameterized by a set of variational parameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: A claim the paper attributes to other work (ref [54], Henriet 2020).

assertions.value: The authors state that the hybrid variational approach might lead to speedups for certain tasks thanks to the exotic correlations that can be encoded in the quantum state, and drastically reduces the coherence time requirements for the computation.
quotes: This approach might lead to speedups for certain tasks thanks to the “exotic” correlations that can be encoded in the quantum state.
this technique enhances the potential of the quantum processors available today by drastically reducing the coherence time requirements for the computation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim, hedged with might, with no evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum phase estimation algorithm [15] offers an exponential speedup over classical methods for finding eigenvalues but remains unpractical for NISQ quantum devices without error-correction, and that a variational procedure was proposed as an alternative.
quotes: Quantum approaches to ﬁnd eigenvalues have previously relied on the quantum phase estimation (QPE) algorithm [15], which oﬀers an exponential speedup over classical methods,but remains unpractical for NISQ quantum devices without error-correction.
assertions.certainty_reason: A claim the paper attributes to other work (ref [15]).

assertions.value: The authors report in the Figure 11 caption that numerical simulations suggest that a NISQ device able to preserve its coherence for circuit depths of a few hundreds could achieve a quantum advantage over the best known classical methods for the Fermi-Hubbard application [63].
quotes: numerical simulations suggest that a NISQ device able to preserve its coherence for circuit depths of a few hundreds could achieve a quantum advantage over the best known classical methods [63].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (ref [63], Cade et al.).

assertions.value: The authors state that the implementation of parallel gates, together with a relatively modest increase of their gate fidelities, will allow neutral atom devices to go beyond the circuit-depth threshold of a few hundreds.
quotes: The implementation of parallel gates associated with a relatively modest increase of our gates’ ﬁdelities will allow neutral atom devices to go beyond this threshold.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product's prospects, with no data shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Jordan-Wigner transformation [59] recovers the true fermionic commutation relations from spin-1/2 operators and maps any electronic Hamiltonian onto a spin Hamiltonian, and that in 2D the mapping comes with an extra difficulty because simple local fermionic Hamiltonians are mapped to non-local spin Hamiltonians and vice versa.
quotes: Jordan and Wigner introduced in Ref. [59] a transformation that recovers the true fermionic commutation relations from spin-1/2 operators.
In 2D, this mapping comes with an extra diﬃculty as simple local fermionic Hamiltonians are mapped to non-local spin Hamiltonians and vice versa.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (ref [59]).

assertions.value: The authors state that neutral atom devices constitute an appealing platform for testing fundamental theories of physics in the high-energy regime, with a development cost four orders of magnitude lower than a particle collider.
quotes: with a development cost four orders of magnitude lower than a particle collider.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product, with no cost data shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that the route to quantum advantage using variational procedures for computational problems seems within reach, and that hardware-efficient variational algorithms that exploit the natively implementable operations are one promising opportunity for improvement.
quotes: the route to quantum advantage using variational procedures for computational problems seems within reach.
One particularly promising opportunity for improvement is the implementation of hardware-eﬃcient variational algorithms
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim, hedged with seems, with no evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the physical interactions encoded in the Hamiltonian constrain the dynamics to only explore independent sets of the graph, leading to an efficient search in the set of possible solutions [72, 54], because Rydberg blockade between atoms closer than r_b corresponds to the independent set constraint.
quotes: the physical interactions encoded in the Hamiltonian constrain the dynamics to only explore independent sets of the graph under study, then leading to an eﬃcient search in the set of possible solutions [72, 54]
This naturally corresponds to the independent set constraint in the graph deﬁned by the atoms, with edges linking atoms that sit at a distance closer than rb.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (refs [72, 54]).

assertions.value: The authors state that gate fidelity and quantum volume are not always the best criteria for assessing the performance of a given quantum hardware on a specific task, and that exploring the same phase space with standard digital gates in a nearest-neighbor architecture would be far more demanding than with atoms.
quotes: well known notions in the ﬁeld of Quantum Information Processing such as gate ﬁdelity or quantum volume are not always the best criteria for assessing the performances of a given quantum hardware on a speciﬁc task.
would be far more demanding than with atoms.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim, with no comparison run in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that a recent preprint from the Google group [73] found that the best performance of a variational algorithm for optimization was achieved on a problem that maps directly to the native hardware layout of the device.
quotes: A recent preprint from the Google group supported this statement, by ﬁnding that the best performance of a variational algorithm for optimization was achieved on a problem that maps directly to the native hardware layout of the device [73].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (ref [73]).

assertions.value: The authors state that the approximate variational algorithms for combinatorial optimization on noisy devices, as initially proposed by Farhi et al., are often referred to in the literature as Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms (QAOA).
quotes: These algorithms are often referred to in the literature as Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms (QAOA).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the term it uses, in Section 3.2.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that an algorithm was recently proposed to solve non-linear partial differential equations [24] using a quantum accelerator within a variational procedure, which makes concrete the prospect of using intermediate-scale quantum processors for non-linear problems on grid sizes beyond the scope of conventional computers.
quotes: An algorithm was recently proposed to solve non-linear partial diﬀerential equations [24] using a quantum accelerator within a variational procedure.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (ref [24]).

assertions.value: The authors state that support vector machines, one of the most successful traditional machine learning approaches for classification, can be cast to a linear system of equations and then solved using matrix inversion, and that the large dimensionality of the vector spaces makes large-scale implementation very resource intensive.
quotes: support vector machines, one of the most successful traditional machine learning approaches for classiﬁcation, can be cast to a linear system of equations, and then be solved using matrix inversion.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement without a citation.

assertions.value: The authors state that, motivated by the prohibitive requirements of linear-algebra-based quantum machine learning, people tried to find other ways to leverage machine learning methods on available NISQ quantum processors, for other purposes than data intensive applications.
quotes: Motivated by these developments, people tried to ﬁnd other ways to leverage Machine Learning methods on available NISQ quantum processors, albeit for other purposes than data intensive applications such as the ones mentioned above.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim with no citation in the sentence.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence limits NISQ QML to purposes other than data-intensive applications, which bears on any use of such devices for large data sets.

assertions.value: The authors state that new quantum applications for machine learning are rapidly developing [8, 78], that several classifiers have been elaborated [79, 80] as well as sampling methods of classically inaccessible systems, and that quantum machine learning for experimental quantum data is another promising direction for quantum sensing or metrology.
quotes: New quantum applications for Machine learning are today rapidly developing [8, 78], and several classiﬁers have been elaborated [79, 80]
Another promising direction concerns the use of Quantum machine learning for experimental quantum data, opening new prospects in enhanced quantum sensing or metrology.

assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no machine learning experiment of its own.

assertions.value: The authors state that fault-tolerant architectures, which implement error-correction procedures, will not be available in the near-future, due to the large overhead in the number of qubits necessary to implement error correction.
quotes: Architectures that implement error-correction procedures are called fault-tolerant; and they will not be available in the near-future, due to the large overhead in the number of qubits necessary to implement error correction.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim with no data in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that recent results from Google [2] have shown that devices without error-correction and with a relatively modest number of qubits can already outperform any classical supercomputer for specific computing tasks.
quotes: recent results from Google [2] have shown that devices without error-correction and with a relatively modest number of qubits can already outperform any classical supercomputer for speciﬁc computing tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (ref [2]).

assertions.value: The authors describe the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) era [1] as one where 50-1,000 qubits devices allow for the exploration of the entanglement frontier, beyond what classical computers can do.
quotes: Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) computing era [1], where 50-1,000 qubits devices allow for the exploration of the entanglement frontier, beyond what classical computers can do.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description the paper attributes to other work (ref [1], Preskill).

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that they give evidence of the intrinsic scalability of neutral atom quantum processors in the 100-1,000 qubits range.
quotes: We give evidence of the intrinsic scalability of neutral atom quantum processors in the 100-1,000 qubits range
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper shows no run at 100 to 1,000 qubits; the evidence it gives is the hardware argument in Section 2 and the 48-qubit routing simulation in Figure 8.

assertions.value: The authors state that coupling several processors with optical interconnects would substantially scale up the number of qubits and make it possible to implement quantum error correcting codes such as the surface code on large system sizes, as one first possible path to a general-purpose fault-tolerant quantum computing device with neutral atoms.
quotes: This multi-core architecture would then allow us to substantially scale up the number of qubits available for computation.
This is one ﬁrst possible path for the construction of a general-purpose fault-tolerant quantum computing device with neutral atoms.
assertions.certainty_reason: A prospect the authors state without data.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper notes that coupling processors needs coherent interfaces between atomic qubits and single photons, which it calls a great experimental challenge (p.24).

assertions.value: The authors state that the infinite dimensional Hilbert space of photons can be used to redundantly encode quantum information without dramatically increasing the number of quantum units, and that photonic or bosonic codes would correspond to a second path towards a fault-tolerant architecture.
quotes: The inﬁnite dimensional Hilbert space of photons can be used to redundantly encode quantum information, without having to dramatically increase the number of quantum units.
would correspond to a second path towards a fault-tolerant architecture.
